questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire, made of a certain material of length-l and area of cross section-a can withstand a maximum load =W without breaking. If, another wire of the same material and cross-sectional area is used with double the original length, what will be the maximum load that the wire can withstand, without breaking?
questions.solution:
Breaking stress is a property of the material and is independent of the dimensions of the wire.

The maximum load a wire can withstand is given by the product of breaking stress and the cross-sectional area.

Maximum load = Breaking stress × Area of cross section

Since the material and the cross-sectional area of the new wire are the same as those of the original wire, the breaking stress and area remain unchanged.

Therefore, the maximum load the wire can withstand remains the same, which is $W$.

Answer: Remains the same =W

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A light rod of length 1 m is suspended from ceiling horizontally by means of two vertical wires of equal length tied to its ends. One of the wires is made of material X and is of cross-section $0.1\ \text{cm}^2$ and the other of material Y of cross-section $0.3\ \text{cm}^2$. A weight is hung from the wire at a point to produce equal strain in the wires. The ratio of Young's moduli of wires A to B is 3:1. The location of the point from one end of the wire is
questions.solution:
Let the length of the rod be $L = 1\ \text{m}$.

Let the weight be suspended at a distance $x$ from the wire of material X.

For rotational equilibrium of the rod, the torques about the point of suspension must balance:

$T_X x = T_Y (1 - x)$

The strain in a wire is given by $\epsilon = \dfrac{T}{AY}$.

Since the strains in both wires are equal:

$\dfrac{T_X}{A_X Y_X} = \dfrac{T_Y}{A_Y Y_Y}$

$\dfrac{T_X}{T_Y} = \dfrac{A_X Y_X}{A_Y Y_Y}$

Given $A_X = 0.1\ \text{cm}^2$, $A_Y = 0.3\ \text{cm}^2$, and $\dfrac{Y_X}{Y_Y} = \dfrac{3}{1}$.

Substituting the values:

$\dfrac{T_X}{T_Y} = \left(\dfrac{0.1}{0.3}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{3}{1}\right) = 1$

This gives $T_X = T_Y$.

Substituting this into the torque equation:

$x = 1 - x$

$2x = 1 \Rightarrow x = 0.5\ \text{m}$

Answer: $0.5\ \text{m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The stress verses strain graph of four metals A,B,C and D are as shown. Which of the graph represent the metal having greatest Young's modulus?
questions.solution:
The Young's modulus $Y$ of a material is defined as the ratio of stress to strain within the elastic limit, which corresponds to the slope of the stress-strain graph.

$Y = \dfrac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}} = \tan(\theta)$

where $\theta$ is the angle that the stress-strain line makes with the strain axis.

Comparing the slopes of the given lines OA, OB, OC, and OD, the line OA makes the largest angle with the strain axis. Therefore, the slope of line OA is the greatest.

Since the slope represents the Young's modulus, the metal represented by graph OA has the greatest Young's modulus.

Answer: Graph OA

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: One end of a nylon rope of length 1 and diameter 10 mm is fixed to free limb. A monkey weighing 100 N jumps to catch the free end and stays there. The change in diameter of the rope is (Young's modulus of the wire is Y and Poisson Ratio is $\sigma$ )
questions.solution:
The Young modulus $Y$ is defined as the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain. The longitudinal stress is $\sigma_{stress} = \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{F}{\pi r^2} = \dfrac{F}{\pi (d/2)^2} = \dfrac{4F}{\pi d^2}$, where $F = 100$ N and $d = 10$ mm = $0.01$ m.

The longitudinal strain is $\epsilon_L = \dfrac{\Delta l}{l} = \dfrac{\sigma_{stress}}{Y} = \dfrac{4F}{\pi d^2 Y}$.

The Poisson ratio $\sigma$ is defined as the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain: $\sigma = - \dfrac{\epsilon_D}{\epsilon_L}$, where $\epsilon_D = \dfrac{\Delta d}{d}$ is the lateral strain.

Therefore, the change in diameter $\Delta d$ is given by $\Delta d = - \sigma \epsilon_L d = - \sigma \left( \dfrac{4F}{\pi d^2 Y} \right) d = - \dfrac{4F \sigma}{\pi d Y}$.

Substituting the given values $F = 100$ N and $d = 0.01$ m:

$\Delta d = - \dfrac{4 \times 100 \times \sigma}{\pi \times 0.01 \times Y} = - \dfrac{400 \sigma}{0.01 \pi Y} = - \dfrac{40000 \sigma}{\pi Y}$.

The magnitude of the change in diameter is $\dfrac{40000 \sigma}{\pi Y}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{40000 \sigma}{\pi Y}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Select the correct statement from the following:
options: The bulk modulus of an ideal liquid is zero
Rubber is more elastic than steel
Shear modulus of an ideal liquid is infinite
The bulk modulus of a perfect rigid body is infinite
questions.solution:
The bulk modulus $B$ is defined as $B = -V \dfrac{dP}{dV}$. For a perfectly rigid body, the change in volume $dV$ is zero for any applied pressure $dP$. Thus, $B = -V \dfrac{dP}{0} = \infty$.

Regarding other options: The bulk modulus of an ideal liquid is finite and positive, not zero. Steel is more elastic than rubber because the Young's modulus of steel is much higher than that of rubber, meaning it requires more stress to produce the same strain. The shear modulus of an ideal liquid is zero because it cannot sustain any shear stress.

Answer: The bulk modulus of a perfect rigid body is infinite

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Young's modulus of the material of wires X and Y are in the ratio $4: 1$ and the areas of cross sections of the wires X and Y are in the ratio 2:1. If the same amount of load is applied to both the wires, the ratio of elongation produced in the wires X and Y will be: (Assume length of the wires X and Y initially are the same)
questions.solution:
The Young's modulus $Y$ is defined as $Y = \dfrac{FL}{A \Delta L}$, where $F$ is the applied force, $L$ is the initial length, $A$ is the cross-sectional area, and $\Delta L$ is the elongation.

Rearranging for elongation, we get $\Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY}$.

Given that the force $F$ and initial length $L$ are the same for both wires X and Y, the elongation $\Delta L$ is inversely proportional to the product of area $A$ and Young's modulus $Y$, i.e., $\Delta L \propto \dfrac{1}{AY}$.

The ratio of elongations is $\dfrac{\Delta L_X}{\Delta L_Y} = \dfrac{A_Y Y_Y}{A_X Y_X}$.

Given $\dfrac{Y_X}{Y_Y} = \dfrac{4}{1}$ and $\dfrac{A_X}{A_Y} = \dfrac{2}{1}$, we substitute these values:

$\dfrac{\Delta L_X}{\Delta L_Y} = \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{1}{4} \right) = \dfrac{1}{8}$.

Therefore, the ratio of elongation produced in wires X and Y is $1:8$.

Answer: $1: 8$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An elevator cable is to have a maximum stress of $7 \times 10^7 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2$ to allow for appropriate safety factors. Its maximum upward acceleration is $1.5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$. If the cable has to support the total weight of 2000 kg of a loaded elevator, the area of cross-section of the cable should be
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} \\ & T_{\max }=m(g+a)=(2000)(9.8+1.5)=22600 \mathrm{~N} \\ \\ & \text { Maximum stress }=\frac{T_{\max }}{\text { Area }} \\ \end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} \\ \therefore \text { Area } & =\frac{T_{\max }}{\text { Maximum stress }}=\frac{22600}{7 \times 10^7} \\ \\ & =3.22 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^2=3.22 \mathrm{~cm}^2 \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The temperature of a wire is doubled. The Young's modulus of elasticity
questions.solution:
Young's modulus of elasticity $Y$ is a material property that depends primarily on the nature of the material and the temperature. When the temperature of a solid increases, the interatomic distances increase due to thermal expansion, which weakens the interatomic forces.

As the temperature increases, the atomic vibrations increase, leading to a decrease in the stiffness of the material. Consequently, the Young's modulus of elasticity decreases with an increase in temperature.

Therefore, when the temperature of a wire is doubled, its Young's modulus of elasticity will decrease.

Answer: Will decrease

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the ratio of lengths, radii and Young's Moduli of steel and brass wires in the figure are $\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}$ and $\mathrm{c}$ respectively, then the corresponding ratio of increase in their lengths would be
questions.solution:
Let $L_s, r_s, Y_s$ be the length, radius, and Young's modulus of the steel wire, and $L_b, r_b, Y_b$ be those of the brass wire. Given ratios are $\dfrac{L_s}{L_b} = a$, $\dfrac{r_s}{r_b} = b$, and $\dfrac{Y_s}{Y_b} = c$.

The tension in the steel wire is $T_s = 2Mg$ (supporting the $2M$ mass). The tension in the brass wire is $T_b = (M + 2M)g = 3Mg$ (supporting both masses).

The elongation $\Delta L$ is given by $\Delta L = \dfrac{TL}{AY} = \dfrac{TL}{\pi r^2 Y}$.

The ratio of increase in lengths is $\dfrac{\Delta L_s}{\Delta L_b} = \dfrac{T_s L_s}{\pi r_s^2 Y_s} \times \dfrac{\pi r_b^2 Y_b}{T_b L_b} = \left( \dfrac{T_s}{T_b} \right) \left( \dfrac{L_s}{L_b} \right) \left( \dfrac{r_b}{r_s} \right)^2 \left( \dfrac{Y_b}{Y_s} \right)$.

Substituting the given values: $\dfrac{T_s}{T_b} = \dfrac{2Mg}{3Mg} = \dfrac{2}{3}$, $\dfrac{L_s}{L_b} = a$, $\dfrac{r_b}{r_s} = \dfrac{1}{b}$, and $\dfrac{Y_b}{Y_s} = \dfrac{1}{c}$.

Therefore, $\dfrac{\Delta L_s}{\Delta L_b} = \left( \dfrac{2}{3} \right) (a) \left( \dfrac{1}{b^2} \right) \left( \dfrac{1}{c} \right) = \dfrac{2a}{3b^2c}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2 a}{3 b^2 c}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two wire of same material having radius in ratio $2: 1$ and lengths in ratio $1: 2$. If same force is applied on them, then ratio of their change in length will be
questions.solution:
Given, ratio of radius of two wires,
$\frac{r_1}{r_2}=\frac{2}{1}$
and ratio in their lengths,
$\frac{l_1}{l_2}=\frac{1}{2}$
When same force is applied on them, then ratio change in their lengths,
$\frac{\Delta l_1}{\Delta l_2}=\text { ? }$
We known that, Young's modulus,
$\begin{gathered}
Y=\frac{F l}{A \Delta l} \Rightarrow \Delta l=\frac{F l}{A Y} \\
\Delta l \propto \frac{l}{A} \\
\therefore \quad \frac{\Delta l_1}{\Delta l_2}=\frac{l_1 / A_1}{l_2 / A_2}=\frac{l_1 A_2}{l_2 A_2} \\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\Delta l_1}{\Delta l_2}=\frac{l_1 / A_1}{r_2^2 / r_1^2}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{8}
\end{gathered}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two wires are made of the same material and have the same volume. The first wire has cross-sectional area $A$ and the second wire has cross-sectional area $3 A$. If the length of the first wire is increased by $\Delta l$ on applying a force $F$, how much force is needed to stretch the second wire by the same amount?
questions.solution:
According to the question, For wire 1 : Area of cross-section $=A_1$, Force applied $=F_1$ and increase in length $=\Delta l$. From the relation of Young's modulus of elasticity, $Y=\frac{F l}{A \Delta l}$ Substituting the values for wire 1 in the above relation, we get
For wire $2:$ Area of cross-section $=A_2$ Force applied $=F_2$ increase in length $=\Delta l$
$\because$ Volume, $V=A l$ or $l=\frac{V}{A}$ Substituting the value of $l$ in Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $Y_1=\frac{F_1 V}{A_1^2 \Delta l} \text { and } Y_2=\frac{F_2 V}{A_2^2 \Delta l}$ As it is given that the wires are made up of same material, i.e. $\quad Y_1=Y_2\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad \frac{F_1 V}{A_1^2 \Delta l}=\frac{F_2 V}{A_2^2 \Delta l} \Rightarrow \frac{F_1}{F_2}= & \frac{A_1^2}{A_2^2}=\frac{A^2}{9 A^2}=\frac{1}{9} \\ & \left(\because A_1=A \text { and } A_2=3 A\right)\end{aligned}$ or $\quad F_2=9 F_1=9 F \quad$ (given, $\left.F_1=F\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A man grows into a giant such that his height increases to 8 times his original height. Assuming that his density remains same, the stress in the leg will change by a factor of
questions.solution:
Let the original height of the man be $h$ and the original cross-sectional area of his legs be $A$. The mass of the man is $m = \rho V$, where $\rho$ is the density and $V$ is the volume. Since the man grows geometrically similar, the volume $V$ is proportional to $h^3$. Thus, $m \propto h^3$.

The stress $\sigma$ in the legs is defined as the force per unit area, $\sigma = \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{mg}{A}$.

Since the man grows geometrically similar, the cross-sectional area $A$ of the legs scales as $h^2$.

Substituting the scaling relations $m \propto h^3$ and $A \propto h^2$ into the stress formula, we get $\sigma \propto \dfrac{h^3}{h^2} = h$.

Given that the height increases by a factor of 8, the stress in the legs will also increase by a factor of 8.

Answer: 8

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two wire of same material having radius in ratio 2 : 1 and lengths in ratio 1: 2. If same force is applied on them, then ratio of their change in length will be
questions.solution:
The change in length $\Delta L$ of a wire is given by the formula $\Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY}$, where $F$ is the applied force, $L$ is the original length, $A$ is the cross-sectional area, and $Y$ is Young's modulus of the material.

Since both wires are made of the same material, $Y$ is the same for both. The force $F$ applied is also the same. Thus, $\Delta L \propto \dfrac{L}{A}$.

The area $A$ is given by $\pi r^2$, so $\Delta L \propto \dfrac{L}{r^2}$.

Given the ratio of radii $r_1 : r_2 = 2 : 1$ and the ratio of lengths $L_1 : L_2 = 1 : 2$, we have:

$\dfrac{\Delta L_1}{\Delta L_2} = \left( \dfrac{L_1}{L_2} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{r_2}{r_1} \right)^2$

Substituting the given values:

$\dfrac{\Delta L_1}{\Delta L_2} = \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{8}$.

Answer: $1: 8$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two wires are made of the same material and have the same volume. The first wire has cross-sectional area $A$ and the second wire has cross-sectional area $3 A$. If the length of the first wire is increased by $\Delta l$ on applying a force $F$, how much force is needed to stretch the second wire by the same amount?
questions.solution:
Let the length and area of the first wire be $L_1$ and $A_1 = A$. Let the length and area of the second wire be $L_2$ and $A_2 = 3A$.

Since the volumes are equal, $V_1 = V_2$, we have $A_1 L_1 = A_2 L_2$. Substituting the given values, $A L_1 = 3A L_2$, which implies $L_1 = 3 L_2$.

The Young modulus $Y$ is the same for both wires. The force $F$ required to produce an extension $\Delta l$ is given by $F = \dfrac{Y A \Delta l}{L}$.

For the first wire, $F = \dfrac{Y A \Delta l}{L_1}$.

For the second wire, let the force be $F'$. Then $F' = \dfrac{Y A_2 \Delta l}{L_2} = \dfrac{Y (3A) \Delta l}{L_2}$.

Substituting $L_2 = \dfrac{L_1}{3}$ into the expression for $F'$, we get $F' = \dfrac{Y (3A) \Delta l}{L_1 / 3} = 9 \times \dfrac{Y A \Delta l}{L_1}$.

Since $F = \dfrac{Y A \Delta l}{L_1}$, it follows that $F' = 9F$.

Answer: 9F

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A copper and a steel wire of same diameter are connected end to end. A deforming force $F_1$ is applied to the wire which causes an elongation of $1 \mathrm{~cm}$. The two wires will have
questions.solution:
Let the copper wire have Young's modulus $Y_C$ and the steel wire have Young's modulus $Y_S$. Both wires have the same diameter, so they have the same cross-sectional area $A$.

When connected end to end and subjected to a deforming force $F_1$, the tension in both wires is the same, equal to $F_1$.

The stress in each wire is given by $\sigma = \dfrac{F_1}{A}$. Since $F_1$ and $A$ are the same for both wires, the stress is the same in both wires.

The strain in each wire is given by $\epsilon = \dfrac{\sigma}{Y}$. Since the Young's moduli $Y_C$ and $Y_S$ are different for copper and steel, the strains $\epsilon_C = \dfrac{F_1}{A Y_C}$ and $\epsilon_S = \dfrac{F_1}{A Y_S}$ will be different.

Therefore, the two wires will have different strains.

Answer: different strain

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A force $F$ applied on the wire of radius $r$ and length $L$ and change in the length of the wire is l. If the same force $F$ is applied on the wire of the same material and radius $4 r$ and length $4 l$, then change in length of the other wire is,
questions.solution:
Young's modulus $Y$ is defined as $Y = \dfrac{F L}{A l}$, where $A = \pi r^2$ is the cross-sectional area of the wire.

For the first wire, $Y = \dfrac{F L}{(\pi r^2) l}$.

For the second wire, let the change in length be $l'$. The material is the same, so $Y$ remains constant. The force is $F$, the radius is $4r$, and the length is $4L$.

$Y = \dfrac{F (4L)}{\pi (4r)^2 l'} = \dfrac{4 F L}{16 \pi r^2 l'} = \dfrac{F L}{4 \pi r^2 l'}$.

Equating the expressions for $Y$:

$\dfrac{F L}{\pi r^2 l} = \dfrac{F L}{4 \pi r^2 l'}$

$\dfrac{1}{l} = \dfrac{1}{4 l'}$

$l' = \dfrac{l}{4}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{l}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Within the elastic limit, the corresponding stress is known as
questions.solution:
In the stress-strain curve of a material, the elastic limit is the maximum stress that a material can withstand without undergoing permanent deformation. The stress corresponding to the elastic limit is defined as the yield strength of the material. Beyond this point, the material begins to deform plastically.

Answer: yield strength

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire is stretched to double of its length. The strain is
questions.solution:
Strain is defined as the ratio of the change in length to the original length of the wire.

Let the original length of the wire be $L$.

The wire is stretched to double its length, so the new length $L' = 2L$.

The change in length $\Delta L = L' - L = 2L - L = L$.

Strain = $\dfrac{\Delta L}{L} = \dfrac{L}{L} = 1$.

Answer: 1

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The Poisson's ratio of a material is $0.1$. If the longitudinal strain of a rod of this material is $10^{-3}$, then the percentage change in the volume of the rod will be
questions.solution:
If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the longitudinal strain and lateral strain respectively, then
$\alpha=\frac{l_{2}-l_{1}}{l_{1}}=10^{-3}=0.001\Rightarrow \quad \frac{l_{2}}{l_{1}}=1.001$
Poisson's ratio, $\sigma=\frac{\text { Lateral strain }}{\text { Longitudinal strain }}=\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & \beta=\sigma \alpha=0 \\ \text { But, } & \beta=\frac{r_{1}-r_{2}}{r_{1}}\end{array}
$\therefore \quad \frac{r_{1}-r_{2}}{n_{1}}=10^{-4}=0.0001\Rightarrow \quad \frac{r_{2}}{r_{1}}=0.9999$
Hence, percentage increase in vol
$=\frac{V_{2}-V_{1}}{V_{1}} \times 100=\frac{\pi r_{2}^{2} l_{2}-\pi r_{1}^{2} l_{1}}{\pi r_{1}^{2} l_{1}} \times 100=\left[\left(\frac{r_{2}}{r_{1}}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{l_{2}}{l_{1}}\right)^{2}-1\right] \times 100=\left[(0.9999)^{2} \times(1.0001)^{2}-1\right] \times 100=0.0008 \times 100=0.08 \%

questions.q: A steel wire of length $4.7 \mathrm{~m}$ and cross-sectional area $3.0 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~m}^{2}$ stretches by the same amount as a copper wire of length $3.5 \mathrm{~m}$ and cross-sectional area of $4.0 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~m}^{2}$ under a given load. What is the ratio of Young's modulus of steel to that of copper?
questions.solution:
Given, for stoul wire,
Area, $A_{1}=3 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~m}^{\text {g }}$
Length, $L_{1}=4.7 \mathrm{~m}$
For copper wire,

A_{2}=4 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~m}^{2}, L_{2}=3.5 \mathrm{~m}

If $\gamma_{1}$ ynd $\gamma_{2}$ be the Young's modulus for the material steel wire und copper wire respectively, then

\begin{aligned}
\frac{\gamma_{1}}{\gamma_{2}} &=\frac{\frac{K_{1} L_{1}}{A_{1} S}}{\frac{r_{2} L_{2}}{A_{2} A l}} \\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\gamma_{1}}{\gamma_{2}} &=\frac{L_{3} A_{2}}{L_{2} A_{1}} \quad\left[\because F_{1}=F_{2}\right] \\
&=\frac{4.7 \times 4 \times 10^{-5}}{35 \times 3 \times 10^{-5}}=1.8 \\
\Rightarrow \quad \gamma_{4}: \gamma_{2} &=1.8: 1
\end{aligned}
